The authority of the “more general and authentic” corrective rule remains underdetermined, and the complete regulative rules are deferred beyond the chapter.
The system is internally coherent as a psychological explanation of variations in conviction.
Its strongest operation is the derivation of multiple evidential distortions from a single model of vivacity transmission.
The historical repair depends on treating initial testimony as proof and subsequent transmission as cognitively homogeneous.
The central fault line is that custom supplies prejudice, philosophical correction, and the standard by which correction is preferred.
The argument depends on inherited premises that belief is vivacity and causal reasoning is customary transition rather than establishing them anew.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if historical homogeneity is treated as a qualification of attenuation and the social cases as tests of the same mechanism.

units.title: Sect. XV. Rules By Which To Judge Of Causes And Effects

items.text: Problem: a priori inspection cannot distinguish actual causal relations from unrestricted causal possibilities.
Core thesis: actual causation is judged through constant conjunction constrained by contiguity, temporal priority, and causal uniformity.
Argument type: reconstructive and methodological, terminating in an anti-scholastic restriction on formal rules.
Movement: a priori causal indeterminacy → empirical criteria → comparative rules → controlled experimentation.
Comparative regularities isolate common causes, differentiating causes, compound effects, and incomplete causes.
Formal rule-production yields to recursive experimental application requiring judgment, perseverance, and widened experience.
Neither causal capacity nor causal incapacity can be determined by mere inspection independent of experience.
No objects are properly contrary except existence and non-existence.
Causation depends wholly on constant conjunction.
Cause and effect are contiguous in space and time.
A cause is temporally prior to its effect.
The same cause always produces the same effect.
The same effect never arises except from the same cause.
Every natural phenomenon is compounded and modified by multiple circumstances.
Decisive causal inquiry requires experimentally separating superfluous circumstances from essential ones.
Every new experiment remains subject to renewed circumstance-analysis.
The operative circumstances of moral phenomena are more numerous, implicit, and obscure than those of natural phenomena.
Increased security requires enlargement of the experimental sphere.
No object is identifiable as a cause or non-cause through mere conception.
No intrinsic classification of objects restricts in advance what may cause what.
Mere occurrence without constant conjunction does not constitute causation.
A non-contiguous or effect-prior relation cannot qualify as causal.
A few experiments cannot establish proportional causal decomposition.
Covariation within an observed range does not license indefinite extrapolation beyond that range.
An object fully present before the effect cannot be the sole complete cause of that effect.
Formal logical precepts neither eliminate experimental judgment nor establish the superiority of scholastic reasoning.
Before experience, anything imaginable remains a possible cause or effect of anything else.
A clear causal experiment licenses projection to phenomena of the same kind without awaiting renewed constant repetition.
When different objects produce the same effect, causation must be assigned to a quality common to them.
When resembling objects produce different effects, the causal difference must be assigned to the circumstance in which they differ.
Adequately repeated proportional covariation indicates a compound effect composed of effects corresponding to parts of the cause.
If a putative cause is fully present while its effect is absent, an auxiliary causal principle is required.
Causal investigation proceeds recursively by varying circumstances, testing essentiality, and submitting each result to renewed variation.
Complex experimental application requires perseverance in inquiry and sagacity in selecting discriminating tests.
Moral inquiry requires broader experimentation because its operative variables are less directly identifiable.
Causal rules regulate inference among experienced regularities rather than disclose intrinsic productive powers.
Within an adequately specified class, apparent irregularity is reassigned to an unisolated difference, compound contribution, or missing co-cause rather than admitted as brute exception.
Experimental correction is structurally open-ended because every control becomes a new object of control.
Causal method cannot be reduced to a self-applying algorithm because no rule independently selects the decisive experimental variation.
Moral inquiry employs the same causal architecture as natural inquiry under conditions of greater variable opacity.
Causal identity shifts from whole objects to experimentally isolated qualities or circumstances.
Objects must not possess causally legible powers available independently of observed conjunction.
Kinds, qualities, and relevant similarities must not be wholly unstable, or comparative causal projection becomes impossible.
Essential circumstances must not be experimentally inseparable in principle.
Causal irregularity must not be brute; it must remain attributable to an undiscovered difference, scope condition, or auxiliary cause.
The obscurity of moral circumstances must not amount to absolute inaccessibility, or enlarged experimentation could provide no increased security.
No observable necessary connection beyond regular conjunction is available to ground causal judgment.
No a priori ontology assigns fixed causal or receptive roles to kinds of objects.
No self-executing logical system can replace experimental discrimination and human judgment.
No terminal experiment closes causal inquiry against further circumstance-analysis.
Non-contrariety + absence of a priori causal discrimination → unrestricted candidate causal relations.
Candidate relation + spatial-temporal contiguity + cause-priority + constant conjunction → causal attribution.
Clear causal instance + cause-effect uniformity → projection to phenomena of the same kind.
Same effect across differing objects → isolate common circumstance; differing effects across resembling objects → isolate differing circumstance.
Repeated proportional part-covariation → compound-effect decomposition; full cause without effect → incomplete-cause diagnosis.
Compound phenomenon → remove or vary circumstance → test essentiality → reanalyze resulting experiment → repeat.
Increasing circumstantial complexity → increasing dependence on perseverance, sagacity, and expanded experimental range.

A priori causal indeterminacy → constant conjunction as empirical ground → spatiotemporal and uniformity rules → comparative isolation → decomposition and completion tests → recursive experimental difficulty → enlargement of experience.
Causal possibility is detached from the conceptual content of objects and left open pending experience.
Actual causes are distinguished from merely possible causes by observed relational structure rather than intrinsic intelligibility.
Resemblance and difference become experimental operators for locating causal circumstances.
Disappointed expectation becomes evidence of an omitted distinction or condition rather than an immediate defeat of causal uniformity.
Proportional covariation reclassifies effects as compounds while restricting inference to adequately tested ranges.
Possession of causal rules is separated from competence in their application.
Moral phenomena are placed on the same causal map as natural phenomena but assigned a higher degree of circumstantial opacity.
Surface: eight rules specify the immediate criteria and comparative tests for judging causes and effects.
Structural: constant conjunction, controlled resemblance, controlled difference, and recursive experimentation isolate operative circumstances within compound phenomena.
Metastrategic: formal logic is subordinated to experimental design, persistence, sagacity, and expansion of the evidential field.
Ontological/Temporal: any non-contradictory object may enter a causal relation, while actual causation takes the form of contiguous, temporally ordered, uniform succession.
The axiom set is sufficient to reconstruct the transition from unrestricted causal possibility to empirical rules and recursive application.
The meanings of same cause, same kind, clear experiment, adequate repetition, full perfection, and essential circumstance remain underdetermined.
Internal coherence depends on stable kinds, causal uniformity, and provisional experimental discriminability.
The structure is strongest in its paired comparative rules and its account of recursive experimental control.
The claim that causation depends wholly on constant conjunction remains imperfectly reconciled with contiguity and priority as additional necessary conditions.
The same-effect/same-cause rule conflicts superficially with different objects producing the same effect; the common-quality rule resolves this only by shifting the unit of causal identity.
Projection from one clear experiment remains in tension with the prohibition on inference from a few experiments because clarity and adequate scope are not formally specified.
The anti-scholastic claim that natural understanding can supply the rules is asserted by contrast rather than generated from the causal axioms.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement but cannot convert its application into a determinate procedure without suppressing the judgment the text declares indispensable.

units.title: Sect. III. Of The Antient Philosophy

items.text: The problem is to explain why collections of distinct and variable qualities are represented as simple, identical substances.
Ancient metaphysical categories are fictions generated by natural operations of imagination rather than discoveries of objective structure.
The argument is genealogical, diagnostic, epistemological, and polemical.
Related qualities → smooth mental transition → imputed identity or simplicity → reflective disclosure of difference → contradiction.
Contradiction → fictive substance → homogeneous matter and substantial forms → accidents → occult qualities.
Vulgar custom is first negated by reflection; false philosophy then preserves the demand for objective connection that reflection has made unintelligible.
Moderate scepticism terminates the impossible search, whereas false philosophy terminates it through meaningless words and anthropomorphic projections.
Unreasonable philosophical fictions can be generated by natural propensities of human nature.
The idea of a body is a mind-formed collection of ideas of distinct sensible qualities found in constant union.
Close relations among ideas produce easy transitions of thought.
The imagination substitutes objects when their modes of affecting thought are similar.
Gradual survey of successive qualities suppresses awareness of change.
Comparison of temporally separated conditions makes their differences salient.
Close relation among coexistent qualities suppresses awareness of composition.
Reflective comparison discloses sensible qualities as distinct, distinguishable, and separable.
Contradiction between natural attribution and reflective disclosure prompts imagination to feign a persisting unifier.
Repeated conjunction of qualities with a supposed substance generates an imagined dependence of those qualities upon it.
Whatever is distinct and separately conceivable may exist separately.
Customary conjunction makes the vulgar mistake difficulty in separating ideas for impossibility in separating objects.
Causal inference rests on observed constant conjunction rather than perceived intrinsic connection.
There is no idea of power or agency as something separate from the mind and inherent in causes.
False philosophy rejects the vulgar perception of connection while retaining the search for connection in matter.
Repetition and verbal resemblance can make unintelligible terms appear secretly meaningful.
Human imagination tends to transfer inward emotions to external objects.
A body is not given as an intrinsically simple object.
Numerical identity is not disclosed by a succession of changing qualities.
Substance is not an intelligible perception, bearer, or explanation.
Substantial forms are not discovered sources of species-specific qualities.
Sensible qualities are not accidents that require an unknown subject of inhesion.
Constant conjunction is not a perceived necessary connection among objects.
Faculties and occult qualities are not meaningful explanations of phenomena.
Sympathy, antipathy, and horror of a vacuum are not warranted affections of external objects.
Related successive qualities are mistaken for one identical object because their gradual survey resembles the survey of an unchanging object.
Related coexistent qualities are mistaken for one simple object because their apprehension resembles a single act of thought.
The same quality-collection appears identical and simple under fluent survey but diverse and composite under reflective comparison.
Substance is invented to preserve identity through variation and unity through composition.
Gradual transformations generate the fiction of homogeneous matter, while salient differences generate the fiction of distinct substantial forms.
The doctrine of accidents converts habitual co-imagination into supposed ontological dependence.
The alleged necessary dependence of qualities on substance collapses once qualities are recognized as separately conceivable.
Occult-quality theory compounds an unintelligible supporting substance with an obscure supported property.
Vulgar custom produces belief in intrinsic connection; reflection removes that belief; false philosophy continues the external search; true philosophy suspends it.
Terms such as faculty and occult quality end inquiry by simulating the presence of an absent idea.
Sympathy, antipathy, and horror of a vacuum externalize affective structures belonging to the observer.
Ancient ontology is a layered repair-system constructed to conceal conflicts produced by incompatible modes of apprehension.
Each metaphysical repair increases ontological complexity while decreasing intelligibility.
False philosophy occupies an unstable middle position: it has enough reflection to destroy vulgar certainty but insufficient scepticism to relinquish the demand that certainty expressed.
Metaphysical terminology functions as cognitive consolation by converting an acknowledged absence of explanation into apparent explanatory closure.
Substantiation and anthropomorphism are variants of one operation: features of the mind’s activity are transferred to external objects.
True philosophy and vulgar thought converge in practical indifference while remaining opposed in epistemic basis.
Similarity between mental operations and object-apprehensions must not entail similarity in the objects apprehended.
Psychological difficulty in separating ideas must not establish metaphysical inseparability.
A posit cannot acquire explanatory legitimacy merely by resolving a contradiction in imagination.
Reflection cannot produce a valid positive metaphysics by preserving the object-side agency that it has rendered inconceivable.
Technical vocabulary has no reserve of meaning independent of an assignable idea.
External nature cannot be presumed to reproduce the emotions and intentions most available to the human mind.
No positively conceivable invariant bearer exists within the system to underwrite identity, simplicity, or cohesion.
No object-side reconciliation of sameness with change or unity with plurality is available; the demanded reconciliation exists only as fiction.
The supposed inner power of causes remains unavailable as an object of thought, leaving the metaphysical interior of causation empty.
No philosophical metalanguage is guaranteed to escape the imaginative mechanisms it diagnoses.
Distinct sensible qualities + constant union → closely related quality-collection.
Successive relation + gradual survey + similarity of mental act → fictive identity.
Coexistent relation + imperceptible transition among parts + similarity of mental act → fictive simplicity.
Distant or analytic comparison → disclosed variation or composition → contradiction → unknown substrate.
Gradual transformation / salient difference → homogeneous matter / substantial form → accident-substrate system.
Constant conjunction → vulgar necessary connection → reflective dissolution → sceptical cessation or false-philosophical search.
Retained demand for agency + absent idea → faculty or occult-quality label → semantic illusion → termination of inquiry.
Internal emotion + projective propensity → affective predicates assigned to nature → anthropomorphic physics.
Quality-collection → smooth transition → identity and simplicity → comparative disruption → substance fiction.
Substance fiction → homogeneous matter and substantial forms → accidents → occult qualities → total incomprehensibility.
Vulgar conjunction → reflective separation → no known connection → false search or moderate scepticism.
Meaningless terminology → simulated explanation → inquiry closure → anthropomorphic projection exposed.
Identity and simplicity are reclassified from object-properties to effects of a mode of mental survey.
Substance, substantial form, accident, and occult quality are relocated from ontology into a genealogy of imaginative repair.
Philosophical sophistication ceases to form a linear ascent: false philosophy becomes an unstable interval between vulgar custom and true scepticism.
Explanatory terms are reclassified as possible mechanisms for stopping inquiry rather than advancing it.
The apparent distance between vulgar thought and true philosophy contracts because both terminate speculation, though for contrary reasons.
Ancient physical principles become legible as projections of affect rather than descriptions of external agency.
Surface: Substance, matter, substantial form, accident, faculty, occult quality, sympathy, and antipathy are subjected to genealogical dissolution.
Structural: Relation, smooth transition, comparison, habit, contradiction-repair, verbal resemblance, and affective projection generate the ancient system.
Metastrategic: Philosophical inquiry is divided between vulgar belief, failed metaphysical repair, and moderate sceptical cessation.
Ontological/Temporal: Unity and identity vary with temporal and analytic perspective, while intrinsic substance and objective causal power remain unavailable to conception.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the section’s genealogy of ancient metaphysical categories.
The wider foundations of the separability principle, causal inference, and moderate scepticism remain underdetermined within this section.
The structure is internally coherent insofar as one mechanism—confusion produced by similar effects on thought—generates both identity and simplicity.
The argument is strongest where alternative modes of survey produce the contradiction that substance is introduced to conceal.
The inference from separate conceivability to possible separate existence is load-bearing but asserted rather than established here.
The genealogy of a belief explains its production but does not by itself establish its falsity; the refutation also depends on the absence of a corresponding idea.
The ranking of vulgar, false, and true philosophy compresses a normative criterion by treating sceptical cessation as justified and verbal cessation as illusory.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the movement from cognitive mechanism through metaphysical proliferation to semantic and anthropomorphic exposure.

units.title: Sect. V. Of The Immateriality Of The Soul

items.text: The central problem is whether perceptions can intelligibly be said to inhere in a material or immaterial substance.
The argument is diagnostic, aporetic, empiricist, and polemically retortive.
The concepts of substance and inhesion must pass the impression-origin and separability tests before the dispute can proceed.
Neither concept passes; the question concerning the soul’s substance is therefore unintelligible rather than merely unresolved.
Perceptions divide into extended and nonspatial kinds, defeating every account that assigns all thought to one uniform spatial or nonspatial subject.
The simple-soul hypothesis reproduces the structural difficulties charged against Spinoza’s simple universal substance.
The movement terminates by separating substance from causation: constant conjunction licenses matter–thought causation while leaving a priori claims about duration without foundation.
Every idea is derived from a precedent impression.
No impression can be identified as the impression of a mental substance.
Whatever is clearly conceived may exist as conceived.
Everything different is distinguishable.
Everything distinguishable is separable by the imagination.
Perceptions are different from one another and from everything else.
Nothing appears requisite to support the existence of a perception.
What remains unknown concerning mind must remain undecided rather than be supplied by speculative hypotheses.
Perceptions are heterogeneous with respect to extension: some are extended and others exist without spatial place.
Whatever has a spatial place must be either extended or an indivisible mathematical point.
A relation of place requires both relata to possess spatial characteristics.
The mind tends to add a new relation to objects already united by other relations.
Every intelligible quality attributed to an external object must be representable through an impression.
No necessary connection between cause and effect is perceived in the ideas of objects.
Constant conjunction constitutes the operative content of the causal relation.
Any pair of real objects is, a priori, susceptible of constant conjunction.
Changes in bodily disposition are constantly conjoined with changes in thought and sentiment.
Every conceivable object can be imagined to become inactive or to be annihilated.
Ignorance concerning mind does not authorize contradictory hypotheses concerning its substance.
The materiality or immateriality of the soul is not an intelligible dispute before substance and inhesion are defined.
Independent existence does not distinguish substance from perception.
Perceptions are not intelligibly defined as accidents requiring an unknown support.
Existence does not universally entail spatial location.
A nonspatial perception is not a mathematical point.
Causal and temporal conjunction is not literal conjunction in place.
Thought is not uniformly extended.
Thought is not uniformly simple, indivisible, and unextended.
A simple immaterial soul is not established by the incompatibility of some perceptions with extension.
Renaming perceptions “actions” rather than “modifications” does not explain their dependence upon substance.
The absence of an apparent conceptual connection between motion and thought does not prove their causal incompatibility.
Simplicity or immateriality does not yield an a priori proof of immortality.
The idea of mental substance lacks legitimate cognitive content.
Because perceptions are separably conceivable and possibly separately existent, defining substance by independent existence makes every perception a substance and destroys the intended distinction.
Inhesion has no intelligible content where no support for perception can be identified as necessary.
The question whether perceptions inhere in material or immaterial substance is composed of terms for which no adequate ideas exist.
Nonspatial perceptions must be admitted as existing nowhere, because treating them as points would make aggregates of them extended.
A nonspatial perception cannot be locally conjoined with an extended body.
Where an extended object and a nonspatial perception are causally and temporally associated, the imagination fabricates spatial conjunction to complete their union.
The attribution of place to nonspatial qualities persists through a conflict between associative imagination and spatially discriminating reason.
Materialism cannot coherently conjoin all thought with extension because some perceptions exclude place.
The simple-soul doctrine cannot coherently conjoin all perceptions with an indivisible subject because some perceptions are themselves extended and divisible.
Any intelligible repugnance between an extended object and a simple substratum transfers to the relation between an extended impression and a simple soul.
The objections to Spinoza’s simple universal substance apply symmetrically to the theological doctrine of a simple thinking substance.
If an action is defined as an inseparable abstract mode of substance, distinct and separable perceptions cannot be explained merely by calling them actions.
No a priori comparison of motion and thought can exclude their causal conjunction.
Bodily motion and disposition may be regarded as actual causes of thought insofar as causation consists in experienced constant conjunction.
Requiring an apparent necessary connection would eliminate every cause; invoking divine agency to repair that absence would make the deity the cause of all volitions and perceptions.
Matter and spirit are equally incapable of supporting an a priori inference to necessary continued existence.
The explanatory burden shifts from identifying a bearer of perceptions to accounting for the relations among perceptions themselves.
The decisive ontological division is not mind against matter but extended perception against nonspatial perception.
Associative relation-completion generates pseudo-ontological placement and allows contradictions to persist under familiar forms of speech.
Materialism and spiritualism become reciprocal overextensions: each universalizes one class of perception into a subject adequate to all perceptions.
Agnosticism concerning mental substance is compatible with an empirical account in which bodily processes cause thought.
Religion is deprived of metaphysical support from substance and simplicity while remaining formally open to moral and analogical arguments.
No impression-transcendent concept may determine the nature of the mind.
Perceptions do not require a numerically identical bearer beneath their differences.
Spatial location is not a universal condition of being.
Theological substance is not exempt from standards applied to materialist or Spinozist substance.
Causal efficacy does not require resemblance, conceptual containment, or a perceivable necessary nexus.
Immaterial simplicity does not contain a principle of necessary persistence.
The unavailable object organizing the dispute is the supposed substratum in which perceptions occur but which can never itself appear as a perception.
No common ontological medium is available through which extended and nonspatial perceptions can be rendered locally homogeneous.
No privileged simple subject survives the reciprocal application of mode–substance objections.
No a priori bridge remains from the vocabulary of soul to the religious conclusion of immortality.
Proposed mental entity → demand originating impression → no impression identifiable → concept excluded.
Difference → distinguishability → imaginative separability → possible separate existence → self-subsistence definition collapses.
Perceptual field → extended/nonspatial partition → spatial relation requires shared spatiality → universal local union fails.
Causal and temporal association → propensity to complete relation → fictive spatial incorporation → concealed contradiction.
Nonspatial perceptions defeat universal extension / extended perceptions defeat universal indivisibility → bilateral closure.
Object-quality mediated by impression → object-level repugnance transfers to impressions → Spinozist and theological hypotheses become structurally equivalent.
Modification renamed action → separability test reapplied → terminological repair fails.
No perceived necessary nexus → causal dilemma → constant conjunction selected → matter–thought causation admitted.
Conceivable inactivity or annihilation → equal contingency of matter and spirit → metaphysical immortality proof suspended.
Undefined substance and inhesion → impression test → separability test → definitional collapse → substance question condemned.
Spatial incompatibility argument → heterogeneous perceptions → associative fiction of place → reciprocal defeat of materialism and immaterialism → Spinozist retortion.
Substance question closed → causal question isolated → necessary connection rejected → constant conjunction installed → matter–thought causation admitted → a priori immortality neutralized.
A metaphysical dispute is reclassified as an unintelligible question generated by cognitively empty terms.
The definition of substance by independent existence collapses the substance–accident distinction at the level of perceptions.
The mind–matter opposition is displaced by a cross-cutting distinction between extended and nonspatial perceptions.
“Existing nowhere” becomes an admissible mode of existence rather than a contradiction.
The apparent location of nonspatial qualities within bodies is reclassified as an associative construction.
Theological immaterialism and Spinozist monism become mutually testable by the same objections.
Causation is detached from substantial ontology and relocated in experienced conjunction.
Immortality is removed from a priori metaphysics without being directly decided by the analysis.
Surface — The soul’s materiality or immateriality is unintelligible, while matter and motion may count as causes of thought.
Structural — Impression-origin, separability, spatial heterogeneity, associative relation-completion, and constant conjunction govern the argument.
Metastrategic — Reciprocal application of identical standards blocks theological polemic from condemning rival substance systems while exempting its own.
Ontological/Temporal — Some beings exist without place; causal possibility exceeds conceptual resemblance; neither matter nor spirit possesses demonstrable necessary duration.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the semantic, spatial, polemical, causal, and temporal movements of the argument.
The positive ontological status of external objects and the precise referent of “matter” remain underdetermined.
The system is internally coherent if the copy principle, conceivability principle, separability principle, and constant-conjunction account are jointly retained.
Its strongest operation is the reciprocal transfer of objections between Spinozist substance and the simple theological soul.
Its greatest compression lies in the claims that all real objects are causally combinable a priori and that conceivability establishes possibility.
A structural fault line remains between condemning substance discourse as unintelligible and continuing to manipulate substance hypotheses for polemical retortion.
The claim of actual matter–thought causation depends on treating bodily and mental covariation as sufficient constant conjunction without further causal individuation.
The religious apology claims neutrality although the metaphysical arguments for immortality have been withdrawn; neutrality depends on isolating moral and analogical arguments from that loss.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the actual movement from conceptual invalidation through reciprocal critique to empirical causal admissibility and temporal suspension.

units.title: Sect. VII. Conclusion Of This Book

items.text: Central problem: whether philosophical inquiry can continue after reflection deprives reason of any independent criterion for assent.
Core thesis: belief is generated by experience, habit, imaginative vivacity, and natural propensity rather than rational self-grounding.
The imagination is simultaneously indispensable to cognition and productive of error, contradiction, and illusion.
Neither unrestricted fancy, purified understanding, nor the rejection of refined reasoning supplies a coherent epistemic rule.
Nature practically dissolves radical skepticism without rationally refuting it.
Philosophy resumes as a natural, pleasurable, comparatively safe inclination governed by skeptical restraint.
Argument type and movement: diagnostic → skeptical self-subversion → affective crisis → natural restoration → pragmatic reconstruction → science of human nature.
Assent to reasoning has no further rational ground beyond a felt propensity.
Experience supplies past conjunctions, and habit projects those conjunctions into the future.
Differential vivacity imparted by imagination is necessary for belief.
Memory, sensory attribution of existence, and causal understanding depend upon imagination or vivacity.
Imagination is an unavoidable but inconstant and fallible cognitive principle.
Causal inference and belief in continued external existence are equally natural and necessary yet can directly conflict.
The represented connection between cause and effect is a customary determination of mind, not a discoverable external power.
Unrestricted assent to imaginative suggestion produces contradiction, obscurity, and error.
Understanding acting solely through its most general principles subverts all evidence, including its own.
A universal prohibition on refined reasoning is itself refined, self-contradictory, and destructive of science.
Embodied sensation, passion, diversion, and social intercourse necessarily restore ordinary belief and action after skeptical crisis.
Reason possesses practical authority only when it is lively and conjoined with propensity.
Curiosity, ambition, and pleasure naturally regenerate philosophical inquiry.
The human mind generally exceeds the sphere of common affairs and therefore must choose among speculative guides.
Philosophy is generally safer than superstition because philosophical error is behaviorally weak while superstition strongly governs conduct.
A stable philosophy must restrain speculative imagination by common practice, experience, and critical examination.
Human nature is the only science of man and the privileged domain of attainable assurance.
True skepticism extends diffidence to both philosophical conviction and philosophical doubt.
Assent is not grounded in an independently demonstrable rational criterion.
Ultimate causal energy is not known as a property residing in external objects.
Every suggestion of imagination is not entitled to assent.
Understanding is not an autonomous faculty separable from imagination.
Refined reasoning cannot be universally prohibited without employing what the prohibition rejects.
Total suspension of belief cannot be permanently sustained.
Nature’s restoration of belief is not a rational refutation of skepticism.
No rational obligation compels philosophical labor against inclination.
Philosophy is not a universal vocation required of every person.
Speciousness, imaginative warmth, and agreeableness do not establish a hypothesis.
Philosophical inquiry does not guarantee truth or certainty.
Positive expressions of certainty do not necessarily imply dogmatism or infallibility.
Belief is psychologically generated rather than rationally self-founded.
The contradiction among natural beliefs cannot be removed by discarding imagination, because imagination is their necessary common source.
Inquiry into ultimate causal power terminates in an account of customary mental transition.
The choice between unrestricted fancy and purified reason becomes a choice between false reason and no reason.
The practical necessity of ordinary belief supplies continuation without epistemic vindication.
Philosophy can continue only through natural inclination rather than purely rational obligation.
Preference for philosophy over superstition is comparative and prudential rather than demonstratively certain.
Philosophical legitimacy depends upon methodological restraint and redirection toward human nature.
Particular assertions may acquire momentary assurance while remaining globally defeasible under skeptical caveat.
Skepticism must recur as self-correction rather than stabilize as permanent disbelief.
The system replaces epistemic foundation with regulated alternation between skeptical reflection and unavoidable natural belief.
Philosophical activity forms a recursive cycle: inquiry intensifies doubt, nature attenuates doubt, and restored curiosity renews inquiry.
Philosophy is justified by comparative harmlessness, natural pleasure, and critical restraint rather than guaranteed access to truth.
The science of human nature is reflexive: fallible faculties investigate the operations and limits of those same faculties.
Epistemic normativity is naturalized because reason’s title to assent depends upon psychological vivacity and propensity.
Human faculties cannot be independently amended or validated by another available cognitive instrument.
The will cannot permanently control assent against habit, sensation, passion, and social life.
Pure reason cannot motivate or govern belief independently of affective force.
The natural necessity of a belief cannot by itself establish that belief’s truth.
Skeptical reasoning cannot coherently exempt its own conclusions from the general fallibility it establishes.
No Archimedean standpoint is available from which reason, imagination, and natural belief can be jointly validated.
No final reconciliation is supplied between contradictory natural principles; their conflict is managed rather than resolved.
Ultimate external power and absolute certainty remain unavailable as terminal objects of inquiry.
Continued philosophy lacks a purely epistemic warrant and survives through inclination, comparative safety, and provisional satisfaction.
Faculty audit: exact reasoning → demand for its ground → discovery of propensity rather than rational warrant.
Belief production: past conjunction → habit → imaginative vivacity → expectation, memory, and existence-attribution.
Contradiction production: common imaginative source → equally natural operations → incompatible conclusions.
Skeptical dilemma: unrestricted fancy → error; purified understanding → self-subversion; prohibition of refinement → self-contradiction.
Affective crisis: sustained reflection → loss of comparative probability → melancholy and cognitive paralysis.
Natural reset: sensation, passion, diversion, and society → attenuation of reflection → restored common belief and action.
Recursive return: restored disposition → curiosity, ambition, and pleasure → renewed philosophical inquiry.

Strategic closure: inevitable speculation → philosophy preferred to superstition → hypotheses restrained by practice and experience → inquiry redirected to human nature → local assertion retained under global diffidence.

Faculty weakness → search for a criterion of assent → imaginative genealogy of belief → conflict among natural principles → self-subversion of purified reason → skeptical delirium → natural restoration → non-foundational preference for philosophy → science of human nature → recursive skeptical caveat.
Reason is reclassified as an operation dependent upon the general and established tendencies of imagination.
Contradiction is relocated from accidental error to the interaction of natural and necessary cognitive operations.
Nature is reclassified from a guarantor of truth to a mechanism that restores practical viability.
Skepticism is reclassified from permanent suspension into diffidence toward both belief and doubt.
The philosophy–superstition distinction is redrawn around psychological force, behavioral danger, and comparative moderation.
Philosophical certainty is divided into momentary local assurance and prohibited global dogmatism.
The object of philosophy shifts from ultimate external powers to the principles and limits of human nature.
Surface: philosophical crisis culminates in the decision whether inquiry should be abandoned or resumed.
Structural: imagination generates belief, contradictory natural operations, skeptical collapse, and practical restoration.
Metastrategic: inquiry is reconstructed as a restrained, inclination-driven, comparatively safe practice directed against superstition and speculative excess.
Ontological/Temporal: past, future, external continuity, and remembered identity are accessible only through present vivacity, customary projection, and recurrent changes of disposition.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the skeptical diagnosis, practical restoration, and qualified return to philosophy.
The system is coherent as an oscillatory practical structure, not as a deductive resolution of skepticism.
Its strongest mechanism is the dependency chain from experience and habit through vivacity to unavoidable belief.
The criterion distinguishing just philosophy from extravagant hypothesis remains only partially specified by moderation, practice, experience, and critical examination.
The transition from reason’s psychological liveliness to its normative title to assent remains under-argued.
The comparative safety of philosophy is a qualified empirical generalization and admits philosophical counterinstances.
The privileging of human nature remains reflexively unstable because the investigating faculties are those already shown to be fallible.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if nature’s cure is retained as practical compulsion rather than epistemic solution.

units.title: Sect. VI Limitations Of This System

items.text: The unrestricted system overgenerates pride and humility from every pleasurable or painful object related to self.
Pride and humility arise only when affective valence and self-relation satisfy additional relational, comparative, social, and temporal conditions.
The argument is diagnostic, restrictive, and reconstructive.
Universal affective law → distinction between joy and self-directed passion → four restrictive thresholds → customary enlargement.
Joy and misery require fewer mediations than pride and humility because self is essential only to the latter pair.
Real happiness and misery can diverge from the distribution of pride and humility.
Pride and humility take self as their object.
Their causes first produce pleasure or pain distinguishable from the resulting self-directed passion.
Pride and humility require a conjoint association of ideas and impressions.
Relations possess variable degrees of force.
Pride requires a closer relation to self than joy requires.
Pride directs attention to both its valenced cause and self, whereas joy properly takes only the valenced cause as its object.
A stronger relation of the cause to another person weakens or destroys its relation to self.
A cause of pride or humility must be peculiar to oneself or shared with only a few persons.
Frequent presentation and long familiarity reduce an object's perceived value.
Human valuation proceeds more through comparison than through intrinsic merit.
A cause of pride or humility must be discernible and obvious both to oneself and to others.
A cause must maintain a relatively constant and durable connection with self.
Imagination anticipates the loss of an inconstant cause and thereby weakens both satisfaction and self-satisfaction.
General rules formed through custom and practice stabilize the valuation and proportional production of passions.
Custom can carry passions beyond the exact bounds warranted by particular circumstances.
Not every pleasurable or painful object related to self produces pride or humility.
Mere relation is insufficient; the relation must be close.
A common or thoroughly familiar good is not ordinarily a sufficient cause of vanity.
A private or indiscernible quality is not fully eligible to produce pride or humility.
A casual or short-lived connection cannot ground a stable inference concerning self.
Intrinsic merit alone does not determine affective value.
Passions are not calibrated anew from each particular object without customary maxims.
Joy is not pride, and pain or misery is not humility.
The proudest person is not necessarily the happiest, and the most humble person is not necessarily the most miserable.
The reality of an evil does not depend on its eligibility to diminish pride.
A weak self-relation can produce joy while failing to produce pride.
Objects too foreign to support vanity can still produce direct pleasure.
Common goods can satisfy without distinguishing their possessor and therefore without producing pride.
Commonness weakens pride twice: the cause lacks singularity, and self gains no comparative distinction through possessing it.
Social invisibility blocks one condition by which a valued quality becomes self-apparent.
A transient cause gives little joy and still less pride because anticipated loss weakens satisfaction and its connection with the durable self.
Customary maxims convert initially irregular and delicate affective principles into comparatively regular responses.
Established classifications can govern passion despite individual circumstances that remove the expected enjoyment.
An evil can cause misery without humility whenever it produces pain but fails the relational, peculiar, public, durable, or rule-governed conditions of self-appraisal.
Degrees of pride and humility cannot serve as direct measures of happiness and misery.
The general system is a gated transformation of pleasure and pain into self-directed passions, not an unconditional causal law.
Pride is more selective than joy because its dual-object structure multiplies the conditions under which affect must operate.
Pride and humility register comparatively legible and temporally stable self-distinction rather than total welfare.
Custom supplies macroscopic regularity to affective mechanisms whose uncultivated operation would remain variable and uncertain.
Common, hidden, transient, or externally caused evils can dominate misery while remaining weakly represented in self-evaluative passion.
The universal mechanism is preserved by restricting its domain of successful operation rather than by abandoning the mechanism itself.
Relation cannot be binary; a mere connection to self cannot have the same force as a close and uncontested connection.
Affective valuation cannot be a transparent registration of intrinsic goodness or badness.
Private consciousness cannot independently determine vanity without comparative and social mediation.
Momentary possession cannot constitute durable evidence of personal excellence or defect.
Untutored passion cannot be presumed to assign stable values correctly on first encounter.
Hedonic condition and self-estimation cannot be coextensive.
General rules cannot remain merely cognitive; the system requires them to organize passion itself.
There is no unmediated passage from the reality of good or evil to a corresponding judgment of self.
There is no guaranteed recognition of suffering within the economy of pride and humility.
There is no self-sufficient measure of personal worth insulated from comparison, publicity, and customary classification.
There is no invariant intrinsic scale capable of explaining the passions independently of familiarity and contrast.
There is no assured equilibrium between particular affective reality and general rules, because custom both regularizes and exceeds particular grounds.
Valenced object → primary pleasure or pain.
Primary affect + relation to self → candidate transition toward pride or humility.
Relational test: closeness sufficient, competing relation subordinate.
Comparative test: cause peculiar, unfamiliar enough to retain value, and capable of distinguishing self.
Discernibility test: cause apparent to self and others.
Temporal test: cause sufficiently constant and proportionate to the duration attributed to self.
Customary-rule operation → stabilized valuation, facilitated passion, possible extension beyond particular warrant.
Successful tests + association of ideas and impressions → pride or humility; failed tests → pleasure or pain without corresponding self-directed passion.
Unrestricted general system → overgeneration problem → necessity of limitations.
Joy/pride distinction → graded relation → peculiarity → public discernibility → temporal constancy.
Variable first-order responses → custom and practice → general maxims → regularized passion.
Qualified causal system → separation of self-estimation from welfare → rejection of any necessary pride–happiness or humility–misery alignment.
A universal causal claim is redrawn as a threshold-dependent transformation model.
Hedonic affect and self-evaluative passion become distinct classes of response.
Relation is reclassified from simple presence into graded, competitive, and interruptible force.
Value is relocated from intrinsic quality alone to familiarity, comparison, rarity, and distinction.
Public appearance becomes a causal condition of self-directed passion rather than an incidental accompaniment.
Real evil is separated from the mechanisms by which evil becomes a basis of humility.
Custom appears simultaneously as an affective regularizer and a source of overextension.
Surface — Five qualifications restrict or enlarge the production of pride and humility from agreeable and disagreeable objects.
Structural — A dual-object passion requires a stronger transition than a direct pleasure or pain and is therefore more vulnerable to failed mediation.
Social — Peculiarity, comparison, shared possession, and visibility to others determine whether a quality distinguishes self.
Metastrategic — General rules explain how delicate causal principles can operate with sufficient regularity to sustain the larger system.
Ontological/Temporal — A relatively durable self functions as the comparator against which transient causes lose self-defining force.
Ontological/Temporal — The reality of good and evil remains independent of whether representational conditions convert them into pride or humility.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the restriction of the general causal system and its concluding separation of welfare from self-estimation.
The exact degree of relational closeness required for pride or humility remains underdetermined.
The causal basis of public discernibility is deferred rather than demonstrated within the section.
The formation and authority of general rules depend on a prior account of custom that is imported in compressed form.
The system is internally coherent where it distinguishes direct pleasure and pain from their conversion into self-directed passion.
Its strongest operation is the explanation of cases in which pleasure or misery persists while pride or humility fails.
A fault line remains between familiarity as a depreciator of value and custom as a stabilizer of value; no priority rule resolves their interaction.
General rules can exceed particular warrant, but their capacity to override the other limitations is not formally bounded.
The claim that the most solid evils often evade humility is structurally licensed but not demonstrated.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the movement from unrestricted law through limitation and enlargement to affective dissociation.

units.title: Sect. XI Of The Love Of Fame

items.text: Problem: explain why reputation governs pride and humility and amplifies their otherwise original causes.
Thesis: love of fame is secondary; praise and blame affect self through sympathetic communication, while authority governs uptake of the judgment.
Another’s expressed sentiment becomes an idea whose vivacity is increased through its relations to the persistently vivid self.
Sufficient vivacity converts the represented sentiment into an impression experienced as one’s own affection.
Variations in esteem, acquaintance, self-concurrence, proximity, and relational convergence test the mechanism against an undifferentiated instinct for fame.
Explanatory-reconstructive movement: reputational effect → sympathy mechanism → application to self-evaluation → differential tests → assimilation of apparent objections.
Ideas and impressions share representational content and differ in force and vivacity.
Consciousness supplies an invariably intimate and maximally lively impression of self.
Relations enable the imagination to transfer vivacity from a present impression to a related idea.
External signs produce an idea of another person’s affection.
Causal inference establishes the represented affection as real.
General human resemblance relates another person’s mental structure to one’s own.
Peculiar resemblance, contiguity, kinship, and acquaintance strengthen the relation between self and another.
A sufficiently enlivened idea of an affection becomes the corresponding impression.
Pride and humility require a self-related source of independent pleasure or pain.
Praise and blame represent another person’s favorable or unfavorable sentiment toward a quality attributed to self.
Reasoning treats another person’s judgment as evidence for the attributed quality.
Evaluative influence increases with the authority accorded to the evaluator.
Praise yields substantial pleasure only when its attribution concurs with, or can alter, the recipient’s own opinion.
Relations amplify sympathy when they converge upon the same evaluator.
Sympathetic impressions remain divided when supporting relations are distributed across different evaluators.
Passion gives additional force to related ideas.
Conscious self-partiality favors confirming evaluations and resists opposing evaluations.
Love of fame is not an original instinct responding equally to every favorable or unfavorable opinion.
National uniformity of sentiment is not adequately explained by soil or climate.
Sympathy is not immediate access to another’s passion; the passion first appears as an idea inferred from signs.
Conversion between idea and impression is not a change in representational content.
Approbation is not equally effective regardless of its source.
Abstract esteem for a quality is not sufficient to make praise pleasurable when possession of that quality is disbelieved.
Relations do not operate merely by existing; they must facilitate associative transition and vivacity transfer.
Relations distributed across different persons do not produce the unified force achieved when they converge upon the same persons.
Blame from a despised or unserious source is not affectively equivalent to credible blame.
Sympathy occurs when signs and causal inference form an idea of another’s sentiment and self-related relations enliven it into the corresponding impression.
Common humanity makes sympathy generally possible, while specific similarity and proximity regulate its intensity.
Praise generates pride when another’s favorable sentiment is sympathetically reproduced, accepted as evidence, and attached as pleasure to a self-related quality.
Preference for the approval of competent judges over indiscriminate approval follows from unequal authority and contradicts an undifferentiated fame instinct.
Intimate acquaintance strengthens approbation by increasing both associative proximity and the evidential weight of judgment.
Praise incongruent with self-attribution cannot ordinarily establish the pleasure required for pride.
Separating kinship from contiguity across different evaluators prevents their contempt from forming a unified sympathetic impression.
Concealment of prior rank suppresses unfavorable comparison in observers and prevents private misfortune from being affectively doubled through sympathy.
Numerical accumulation can compensate for low individual esteem by conferring aggregate authority upon popular opinion.
Undeserved praise can please when imagination fabricates a provisional self-attribution and sympathetic agreement stabilizes it.
Contempt can wound without securing assent because the sympathetically received passion conflicts with antecedent pride; the effect disappears when the critic lacks credibility or seriousness.
Reputation is mediated self-affection: an external evaluation becomes causally effective only by being internally reproduced.
The self is both the source of vivacity and the eventual object of the sentiment that vivacity imports, producing a recursive self–other–self circuit.
Social evaluation has a relational topology: proximity, authority, convergence, separation, and multiplicity determine affective force more than bare evaluative content.
Individual self-esteem and collective uniformity are generated by the same mechanism of communicated sentiment.
Social opposition can alter affect without altering belief because sympathetic reception and intellectual assent are separable.
The distinction between original and secondary causes of pride is functionally porous because communicated opinion amplifies the qualities nominally capable of producing pride independently.
Other minds cannot be affectively sealed from one another.
Ideas cannot be permanently separated from impressions by an absolute difference of kind.
Self-evaluation cannot be sovereign or insulated from socially transmitted sentiment.
Evaluative influence cannot be reduced to propositional content independently of relational configuration.
Relations cannot be inert classifications; they must alter transitions and vivacity.
Reason cannot remain neutral when its judgments are connected with passion and self-partiality.
The system forecloses an autonomous self whose passions originate wholly within its private judgment.
Fame has no independent affective substance apart from communicated sentiments and their authority.
A neutral tribunal of self-worth is unavailable because both external testimony and internal judgment are modulated by passion.
Expression → external sign → causal certification → idea of another’s sentiment.
Vivid self-impression → human resemblance plus contingent relations → associative transition → transferred vivacity.
Enlivened idea → idea–impression threshold crossed → corresponding affection reproduced → sympathy.
Evaluative sentiment about self → sympathetic affect plus testimonial evidence → pleasure or pain attached to a self-quality → pride or humility.
Judge authority plus relational proximity plus self-concurrence plus relational convergence plus numerical accumulation → degree of reputational influence.
Distance plus disesteem plus nonconcurrence plus divided relations plus perceived jest → attenuation or interruption of reputational influence.
Apparent counterexample → identify compensating authority, imaginative supplementation, or passion-conflict → return variation to the sympathy mechanism.

Reputational power → rejection of undifferentiated fame instinct → general sympathy principle → vivacity-transfer mechanism → application to praise and blame → differential phenomena → assimilation of objections → communication-of-sentiments thesis.
Fame is reclassified from an original appetite into a secondary effect of sympathetic communication.
Opinions are reclassified as both propositions carrying evidential authority and sentiments capable of affective transmission.
Resemblance, contiguity, kinship, and acquaintance become conductors of vivacity rather than merely descriptive relations.
Reputation becomes a topological phenomenon governed by the arrangement of evaluators around the self.
Affective injury is separated from intellectual assent, making resisted contempt psychologically operative.
Relocation, anonymity, and concealment become mechanisms for altering shame without altering the underlying material condition.
Surface: praise, blame, reputation, and infamy produce differential pride and humiliation.
Structural: relational networks regulate the conversion of others’ sentiments into self-affection.
Metastrategic: controlled variations in authority, proximity, concurrence, and relational convergence test sympathy against the rival instinct model.
Ontological/Temporal: ideas and impressions occupy a continuum of vivacity, while sympathy unfolds as the compressed sequence sign → idea → enlivening → impression.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from sympathy’s perceptual mechanism to the secondary production of pride and humility through reputation.
The quantitative threshold for idea–impression conversion and the relative weights of authority and relational proximity remain underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent across variations in evaluator status, acquaintance, concurrence, and relational distribution.
Its strongest discriminator is the unequal influence of opinions that an original, undifferentiated fame instinct would treat equally.
Reconstruction depends on the prior theories of association and of independent pleasure or pain as causes of pride and humility.
The case of consciously undeserved praise requires imaginative fiction to preserve the concurrence condition, introducing an auxiliary mechanism.
The response of pride to rejected contempt leaves an unresolved boundary between communication of sentiment and adoption of judgment.
The claim of lossless conversion under perfected sympathy coexists with graded ordinary influence without a specified threshold or measure.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s real movement only if these qualifications remain visible rather than being absorbed into an unrestricted sympathy principle.
Problem: reconcile apparent exceptions to the pleasure–pain account of love and hatred and explain their conjunction with further passions.
Core thesis: affection arises when pleasure or uneasiness is joined to a sufficiently vivid and durable imaginative relation to a person.
Argument type: diagnostic, eliminative, and reconstructive.
Momentary causation → intention/durability distinction → explanation of transient versus lasting passion.
Relation, acquaintance, and resemblance → increased vivacity → agreeable agitation → affection, modulated by directional association.
Candidate causes of wealth-esteem → elimination of object-pleasure and expected advantage as primary → sympathy → recursive amplification.
Passion-mixture → rejection of identity between love and benevolence → contingent natural conjunction → constructive sympathy as the basis of pity.
Love and hatred vary in valence and intensity with the pleasure or uneasiness received from another.
Love and hatred require both a relation of ideas to a person and a relation of impressions between pleasure or pain and passion.
An enduring personal quality connects its pleasure or uneasiness to the person independently of intention.
A momentary action requires intention to remain connected to its author after the action disappears.
Intention intensifies injury or service by signifying contempt, hatred, kindness, or esteem toward the recipient.
A sufficiently forceful pleasure or pain can activate passion despite only a weak relation of ideas to its personal cause.
An established passion tends to generate judgments that prevent its diminution.
Ideas and impressions differ principally in force and vivacity, permitting a sufficiently lively idea to become an impression.
Lively conceptions are agreeable, and conceptions of passions produce especially strong mental agitation.
Relation, acquaintance, and resemblance increase the force of conception through association, custom, or dispositional correspondence.
A personal relation is strongest when imaginative transition between its terms is easy in both directions.
Sympathy converts a vivid idea of another’s sentiment into a corresponding impression through resemblance between persons.
Extension by a general rule requires predominantly uniform experience connecting the relevant condition and effect.
Possession, power, and utility produce actual or represented satisfaction in their possessor or beneficiary.
Power and riches elicit esteem even where the observer can expect no benefit from their possessor.
Sentiments communicated between persons can be reciprocally reflected and amplified.
Passions can blend into a compound impression, whereas ideas combine without losing their distinctness.
Love and hatred stand in an original but contingent conjunction with benevolence and anger rather than in identity with them.
Sympathy can construct the passion customarily associated with a condition even when that passion is absent from the person observed.
Imaginative proximity and contrast intensify sympathetically constructed emotion.
Mere causal production of pleasure or pain is not sufficient for durable love or hatred.
Intention is not universally necessary for affection toward personal qualities.
Accidental and involuntary harm is not incapable of producing immediate anger.
Acknowledged justice does not necessarily extinguish anger caused by harm.
The opinion of iniquity is not always the antecedent cause of hatred.
Affection arising from relation or acquaintance is not proportioned solely to objective merit.
Logical reciprocity between objects does not guarantee equal psychological transition in both directions.
Esteem for riches is not principally caused by contemplation of agreeable possessions.
Esteem for riches is not principally caused by expected personal advantage or a general rule derived from such expectation.
Love is not identical with desire for another’s happiness, nor hatred with desire for another’s misery.
The conjunction of love with benevolence and hatred with anger is not conceptually necessary.
Pity does not require antecedent friendship or reflection on one’s own vulnerability to misfortune.
Sympathy does not require the observed person actually to feel the passion communicated to the observer.
Enduring qualities produce stable affection without design, whereas transient actions require design to disclose enduring character.
Intention strengthens passion twice: by connecting the action to the person and by adding communicated esteem or contempt to its effect.
Accidental harm can produce violent but short-lived anger because the impression remains strong while the personal relation remains weak.
Recognized justice diminishes but need not erase anger because it opposes the painful impression without annihilating it.
Harm can first produce hatred, after which hatred produces an opinion of injury that stabilizes it.
Relation and acquaintance produce affection by making the related or familiar person unusually vivid and therefore agreeable to contemplate.
Resemblance facilitates affection both by transferring vivacity and by predisposing the observer toward the corresponding emotion.
A competing relation weakens an existing tie when it redirects imagination and obstructs the return transition.
Agreeable possessions generate esteem chiefly when imagination passes from the possessions to the satisfaction of their possessor.
Expected advantage cannot principally explain wealth-esteem because esteem persists where benefit is impossible and the uniformity required for a general rule is absent.
Sympathy remains the general cause of wealth-esteem because it communicates the proprietor’s satisfaction independently of benefit to the observer.
The perceived beauty of utility is pleasure communicated from the beneficiary rather than pleasure intrinsic to sensible form.
Wealth produces a feedback circuit in which possession causes satisfaction, communicated satisfaction causes esteem, and perceived esteem increases the possessor’s satisfaction.
Love and hatred acquire practical tendencies through their conjunction with benevolence and anger, not through their own conceptual essence.
Pity for strangers follows from the general human resemblance that permits their sorrow to become a vivid impression in the observer.
An observed misfortune can produce stronger pity when the sufferer feels less sorrow because general expectation supplies the absent passion and contrast heightens it.
Personal attribution is temporally organized: durable passion requires either a durable quality or a sign of durable character.
Moral accusation can function as an endogenous preservation-mechanism of prior affect rather than as its independent rational cause.
Kinship, acquaintance, resemblance, and sympathy form one economy of transmitted vivacity whose recurrent output is affection.
Social attachment depends on the topology of imaginative passage, not merely on the existence of an objective relation.
Economic rank and utility-based beauty are affective appropriations of satisfaction located initially in another person.
Wealth reproduces its own desirability through recursive exchanges between possessed power, observer esteem, and proprietary vanity.
The benevolent or destructive direction of love and hatred is naturally installed but not logically or morally entailed by those passions.
Sympathy is a constructive simulation capable of exceeding, supplementing, or replacing the actual emotion of its apparent source.
Rational judgment of guilt cannot be the exclusive ground of anger or hatred.
Deliberate intention cannot be the universal gate through which affective attribution passes.
Objective merit cannot independently determine affection against the force of familiarity and associative vivacity.
The mind cannot be affectively self-sufficient; its animation depends on lively relations to external objects and other minds.
Relations cannot be treated as static, symmetrical properties without regard to the direction and interruption of imaginative movement.
Social esteem cannot be reduced to calculated self-interest or probable exchange.
The practical tendencies of passions cannot all be deduced from their conceptual content; some conjunctions remain irreducibly constitutional.
Sympathetic communication cannot be assumed to reproduce another’s inner state with veridical fidelity.
An affectively neutral standpoint from which persons are judged independently of pleasure, pain, association, and prior passion is unavailable within the system.
Intrinsic social or aesthetic value independent of communicated satisfaction is structurally displaced.
No necessary moral order guarantees that love seeks happiness or hatred seeks misery; the alignment rests on contingent nature.
Transparent correspondence between the actual emotion of one mind and the sympathetic emotion of another is foreclosed.
A closed individual mind capable of sustaining pleasure, passion, and value without reflective dependence on other minds is excluded.
Pleasure or uneasiness from another → agreeable or disagreeable impression.
Enduring quality ∨ intention-as-character-sign → strong person-relation; momentary accident → weak person-relation.
Impression-relation × person-relation → love or hatred; strong impression × weak relation → acute but unstable passion.
Intention → communicated esteem or contempt → vanity or mortification → amplified affection.
Pain-generated passion → threat of diminution by innocence or justice → justificatory injury-judgment → partial stabilization.
Self-vivacity → relation, custom, or resemblance → lively idea of another → agreeable agitation → affection.
Easy outward transition + easy return → strong tie; competing transition + obstructed return → weakened tie.
Possession or power → proprietor satisfaction → sympathetic esteem → perceived esteem → vanity → renewed satisfaction and esteem.
Love or hatred + original constitutional coupling → benevolence or anger → blended compound affection.
Observed condition + human resemblance + customary affect-rule + proximity or contrast → vivid constructed impression → pity despite absent original sorrow.
Pleasure–pain rule → intentionality difficulty → quality/action distinction → explanation of passion duration → passion-generated injury judgment.
Love of relations and acquaintance → search for common cause → force and vivacity → reciprocal-transition model.
Wealth-esteem → competing causal hypotheses → failure of direct object-pleasure and expected advantage → sympathy → recursive status amplification.
Compound passions → identity hypothesis → experiential rejection → original contingent conjunction of love with benevolence and hatred with anger.
Pity without friendship → sympathy through resemblance → communication of sorrow → passion without an actual original → constructive imagination.
Agency is reclassified from immediate causal authorship to durable attribution through character or intention.
The judgment of injury becomes potentially an effect of hatred rather than its necessary antecedent.
Kinship, familiarity, and resemblance become variants of one vivacity-producing mechanism.
Relations become directional pathways of imagination rather than merely reciprocal logical connections.
Esteem for wealth is relocated from rational advantage to vicarious participation in proprietary satisfaction.
Utility-based beauty is relocated from sensible form to sympathetic apprehension of another’s benefit.
Love and hatred are separated from the benevolent and destructive desires that ordinarily accompany them.
Sympathy is expanded from emotional transmission to affective construction under association, general rules, and contrast.
Surface: variations in anger, affection, social esteem, benevolence, and pity are treated as test cases for the passion-system.
Structural: double relations, force and vivacity, directional association, sympathy, and recursive reflection generate the observed passions.
Metastrategic: apparent counterexamples are converted into discriminating tests that eliminate rival mechanisms and qualify the governing hypothesis.
Ontological/Temporal: ideas and impressions differ by degree of force; enduring qualities sustain personal attribution, while transient events produce unstable passions unless mediated by intention.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the principal transitions from personal causation through association and sympathy to compound affection and pity.
Reconstruction preserves the operative movement: anomaly → distinction → rival elimination → revised mechanism → extension.
Internal coherence depends on accepting force and vivacity as the common currency connecting association, pleasure, impression, and passion.
The structure is strongest where rival explanations generate discriminating cases, especially intention, impossible benefit, and love–desire identity.
The relative weights of harm, justice, intention, associative strength, and individual disposition remain underdetermined.
Appeal to an original constitutional conjunction preserves the phenomenon of benevolence and anger at the cost of further causal derivation.
Sympathy shifts from reproducing actual emotion to constructing absent emotion without a fully specified criterion governing the shift.
Malice is classified as a secondary affection but is not derived with the completeness given to pity.
Compression removes illustrative cases without removing the distinctions, eliminations, feedback structures, or terminal tensions required to regenerate the argument.

units.title: Sect. VIII Of Malice And Envy

items.text: Problem: explain unprovoked pleasure in another’s misery and pain in another’s enjoyment.
Core thesis: malice and envy arise when comparison converts another’s condition into an inverse estimate of one’s own.
Argument type: reconstructive psychological diagnosis grounded in affective succession and associative transition.
Comparative judgments vary because comparison alters an idea’s attendant emotion, which custom then attributes to the object.
Comparison becomes affectively operative only where relations permit easy transition between ideas and their impressions.
Movement: comparative distortion → altered self-estimate → reverse affect → malice/envy differentiation → relation-conditioned general law.
Human sentiments ordinarily assign value through comparison rather than intrinsic assessment.
Every sensed object or imagined idea is accompanied by an emotion proportioned to it.
A succeeding emotion is magnified or diminished by contrast with the preceding emotion.
Habitual general rules carry the mind from a degree of emotion to the object’s customary corresponding degree.
Satisfaction with one’s condition varies with its apparent fortune.
In comparison, one term alters the felt value of the other in a direction contrary to its own direct affective effect.
Associative relation between ideas enables an easy transition of imagination.
Easy transition preserves the first object’s impression during passage to the second.
Preserved impressions can modify one another through comparison or affective contrariety.
Envy is pain produced when another’s present enjoyment comparatively diminishes one’s own apparent condition.
Malice is the unprovoked desire to produce another’s misery for the pleasure of comparative self-advantage.
A predominant passion assimilates affective additions to its own direction.
Malice is not hatred caused by antecedent offense or injury.
Affective judgment is not governed chiefly by reason or intrinsic value.
Comparative variation is not produced by alteration of the immediate impression, image, or idea.
The direct survey of another’s condition is not affectively equivalent to comparison with that condition.
Envy is not proportionate to the absolute magnitude of another’s superiority.
Proximity in merit alone is not sufficient for envy without supporting relations.
Unrelated ideas cannot substantially affect one another merely through juxtaposition.
Contrary passions do not encounter or neutralize one another when their objects remain associatively separate.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A2 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A4) Comparison can change judgment while leaving representation unchanged because contrast alters the attendant emotion and custom attributes that alteration to the object.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A5 + CH_THN_SVME:A6) Another’s misery elevates one’s apparent happiness and produces pleasure, while another’s happiness diminishes it and produces pain.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A6) The same misery can be painful under direct survey and pleasurable under comparative survey.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A5) Past pain becomes agreeable when contrasted with present satisfaction, while past pleasure becomes painful when contrasted with present deficiency.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A12) Self-inflicted suffering can remove a contrast that would otherwise intensify predominant grief or the imagined punishment of remorse.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A5 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) An inferior’s approach converts decreased comparative pleasure into positive pain by comparing the reduced advantage with its former degree.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A9 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) Nearby or resembling rivals provoke more envy than remote superiors because proximity sustains the transition required for comparison.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A9) Separating related objects into distinct conceptual units prevents their attendant passions from influencing or contradicting one another.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) The mind seeks relief from related superiority either by breaking the association or by removing the superiority itself.
Evaluative magnitude is relationally produced even where the perceived object and its representation remain invariant.
Malice converts another’s suffering into an instrument for changing one’s own apparent position.
Envy follows associative proximity more reliably than absolute inequality.
